chapters.title: Chapter 3: Signal Decay and Crowding: When an Edge Gets Discovered

lessons.title: Spotting Crowding Before It Shows Up in Your Returns

children.text: The case study in the last lesson showed what crowding looks like once it hits your P&L. This closing lesson of the chapter is about catching it earlier than that, using indicators that move before your returns do, not after.
Why Your Own Returns Are the Worst Early Warning Signal

By the time your own P&L clearly shows crowding damage, the unwind has usually already started, and you are reacting from inside it rather than watching it approach. Waiting for returns to confirm a problem means you find out last, not first. Everything in this lesson is about tracking indicators upstream of your own return series.

cells: A steady decline over multiple periods, even while total returns still look acceptable, is often the earliest quantitative sign
Monthly, using a rolling 6 to 12 month window
Rising correlation with a published momentum, value, or quality index suggests your edge increasingly overlaps with a widely followed one
Your holdings moving sharply together with no shared fundamental trigger suggests shared positioning rather than shared fundamentals
Volume and spread anomalies on rebalance dates
Unusual trading activity concentrated on known dates, such as index reconstitution or quarter end, when many similar strategies trade together
Public attention to the underlying idea
Growing course content, blog posts, or social media threads describing your exact strategy logic is a leading indicator that more capital is likely to follow

children.text: This does not need to be sophisticated. A monthly review of rolling IC, correlation to one or two published factor indices, and a simple note on any new public attention to your strategy's core idea is often enough to catch a multi-month decay trend well before it turns into a multi-day crash. The value is in the habit of checking on a schedule, not in the complexity of the tracking.

body.title: Monthly Crowding Check
steps: Has my rolling 6 to 12 month Information Coefficient declined for two or more consecutive periods?
Has my strategy's correlation to any published factor index risen meaningfully since last quarter?
Did any of my core holdings move sharply together on a date with no shared company-specific news?
Was there unusual volume or spread behavior around the last known rebalancing date?
Has the core logic behind my strategy shown up in new public content, courses, or widely shared posts since I last checked?

children.text: What to Do When You Spot Early Signs

None of these signs alone means abandon the strategy immediately. A graduated response usually serves better than an all-or-nothing one: trim position sizing or leverage rather than closing the book outright, look for signal variations that are less publicly documented, and tighten risk limits so a crowded unwind cannot do as much damage if one does arrive.

body.text: Capacity is not a fixed number computed once at launch. As alpha decays and crowding grows, a strategy's effective capacity ceiling can fall even while its AUM stays exactly the same. Chapter 4 treats a capacity estimate as a living number to revisit on a schedule, not a one-time calculation you file away and forget.

Your P&L is the last place crowding shows up, not the first. Rolling IC, factor correlation, and unusual co-movement all move earlier, and a habit of checking them on a schedule buys you time that reacting to your own returns never will.

points: Your own return series is a lagging indicator of crowding, since by the time it clearly shows damage, an unwind is typically already underway.

Five practical leading indicators, rolling IC, factor correlation, unexplained co-movement, rebalance-date anomalies, and public attention to the strategy's logic, can be tracked on a simple monthly schedule.
A graduated response, trimming size, diversifying signal sources, and tightening risk limits, is usually more appropriate than an immediate full exit at the first sign of decay or crowding.
Capacity should be treated as a living estimate that can fall over time even without any change in AUM, a theme Chapter 4 builds directly on.
